I guess this is in the vein of what libgpiod does with its separate libraries, but I'd like to understand if that's definitely the right direction, rather than providing one library with both C and C++ APIs.

I don't have any preference there.

Probably easier for the user to have a single library.

But since the C++ binding is optional then libpldm != libpldm.

If it's not optional then the size of the library might be too big for some people because of the additional code. Not sure if size is a big topic.

Let me know what you want to go with 👍

Well, we already have the meson option to drop the transport APIs and implementations from the build. I think the specific approach could be more fine-grained, but that depends on people actually caring about it too.

Checked with ```DESTDIR=/tmp/install meson install``` that only the headers we want are installed.

The newer libpldm iterator-style APIs are a big improvement. We should do the conversion where necessary.

Implementation of these methods shouldn't be doing any raw indexing into the provided buffer. That's the responsibility of the C APIs.

Makes sense. Agree that the stuff from libpldm should not be re-implemented in the binding.

Since the firmware_update.h header is quite big, can you suggest which functions/macros would be appropriate? I have split the functions here up into more smaller functions, so the indentation should be less and easier to see which does what.

I found several macros (ew, C macros) of the form ```foreach_pldm_*``` in the libpldm headers, but unsure if they are complete (covering all structs) and which is appropriate to use.

So to set expectations, currently I don't plan to merge the C++ binding without making improvements to the C API to eliminate most of the implementation of these APIs.

Sorry, my comment wasn't as specific as it should have been. I was not concerned about the use of `std::format`.

The code is parsing the provided message byte buffer. That's not the responsibility of the C++ binding, that's the core responsibility of the (C) library. Internally, libpldm provides a number of mechanisms to ensure spatial memory safety and correct handling of endianness that are both ergonomic to use and generate code with good performance. Specifically, the APIs provided by `src/msgbuf.h`. Those are completely dodged by this implementation. This is not code I wish to maintain. Reviewing stuff like this requires constant vigilance to prevent CVEs (which I will fail at), whereas use of the msgbuf APIs allows me to assume no unsafe accesses are performed or incorrect representations generated, or if there are bugs of this nature, they can be fixed centrally to the benefit of the rest of the library implementation.

There should be C APIs to extract the necessary data to (unpacked) C structs, and from there you can populate your C++ classes (though, possibly it would make sense to embed the C struct as a member in the class). If we do not yet have C APIs to do the job, then it's a deficiency of the (C) library that must first be fixed.

Adding this comment at the top as I have a few questions about the design-

1. Considering the platform might support non-PLDM updaters, if a platform implements multiple code updaters, does each updater need to parse the package independently? This would imply running the same parsing logic and decode APIs multiple times in the update flow.

2. The PackageIntegrity check needs to be integrated with the parsing logic. If the libpldm API implements this functionality, does it mean the integrity check will be performed every time different updaters parse the package?

Thanks for your interest in this patch 😊

> If a platform implements multiple code updaters, does each updater need to parse the package independently? 

I believe it depends on the package routing. If you go via bmcweb/redfish then the update is performed via dbus and the dbus fw inventory. In the new design 
https://github.com/openbmc/docs/blob/master/designs/code-update.md
the package has PLDM format. So if the component is not managed by the specific code updater, it may not even receive the update package.

Currently i do not know of any plans to have a front-end for the pldm package which does the parsing. So each updater to receive the package may need to parse it.

However, parsing the PLDM package is easily done with the C++ binding.

> This would imply running the same parsing logic and decode APIs multiple times in the update flow.

If that happens for some reason, i do not see it as a problem. Parsing a PLDM package is quite efficient. And firmware update is not something that happens very often.

> The PackageIntegrity check needs to be integrated with the parsing logic. If the libpldm API implements this functionality, does it mean the integrity check will be performed every time different updaters parse the package?

Yes, the integrity has to be checked to avoid processing a corrupted pldm package or indexing out of bounds.


Consider the following script

```

curl -k ${creds} \
	-H "Content-Type:multipart/form-data" \
	-X POST \
	-F UpdateParameters="{\"Targets\":[\"/redfish/v1/UpdateService/FirmwareInventory/${target}\"],\"@Redfish.OperationApplyTime\":\"Immediate\"};type=application/json" \
	-F "UpdateFile=@${fwpath};type=application/octet-stream" \
	https://${bmc}/redfish/v1/UpdateService/update
```

in which i target a single firmware inventory item. In that case, the PLDM parsing should only happen once.

So if you target your pldm fw update package correctly, it should not be processed more often than required.

If you do not know which devices from the fw inventory should receive the update package, you can also target it to all of them, and the update daemons should figure out if the package is intended for that device or not.

That would be the case you described where the PLDM fw update package is processed multiple times.

I don't understand the question. The definition of ApplicableComponents in DSP0267 v1.3.0 Table 4 is:

> Bitmap of which firmware components are applicable to FDs which match this Device Identifier
record. A set bit N indicates the Nth (0-based) component in the payload (which is described by the Nth entry in the component information area of the package header) is applicable to this device.

The whole point is to associate component images with a firmware device.

I'm proposing we stash the bitmap as-is for now, until we've processed all the component images. After that can create a structure that directly lists the component images for a given firmware device, rather than leaving it to the library consumer to resolve the images from the bitmap themselves. That way we're not exposing this variable-length bitmap with slightly troubling semantics (regarding the potential discrepancy between the available bits and the number of component images), or just a raw list of indexes. We can use [std::reference_wrapper](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/functional/reference_wrapper.html) to maintain the actual component image infos in a canonical list and references to these objects in the list maintained in the firmware device object.

We can do the ```std::reference_wrapper``` but it will require our returned object to be stationary. Any copying would invalidate the references.

So i am tending towards ```std::unique_ptr``` here to provide this guarantee.

When representing the structure of the PLDM packgage, we can use classes/structs or the plain STL containers.

I am using STL containers since that what was the original PackageParser was doing.

The upside is that we do not have to define any constructors or worry about encapsulation. And all of the STL algorithms work well with the STL containers.

The downside is that we expose the complete public API of the various STL containers which may not be needed. And we don't have the opportunity to add our own member functions.

When using STL containers, we cannot name any members so we may need type aliases to prevent any confusion.

The point about STL containers is fine, but much of what's in this header are aliases for standard integer types. Why? And why are we decomposing these things from their natural representation as a struct into tuples of aliased types? That's not an ergonomioc API in my opinion, and is not something I intend to maintain.

We don't have to swallow whatever API design was done in pldmd. We can try to do better.
